nameStory: Slippery Jill gets its common name from its notably slimy, slippery cap surface when wet - so slick you might struggle to get a good grip on it! The "Jill" part follows the naming tradition of giving these slippery mushrooms human names, like its close relative the Slippery Jack.
description: Slippery Jill is a medium-sized bolete mushroom with a dingy yellow to brownish cap that grows up to 3 inches wide and feels distinctly slimy when moist. Instead of gills, it has tiny pores underneath that start yellow and turn olive-brown with age. The stem can reach 4 inches tall and is decorated with reddish-brown dotted bumps, plus young specimens have a grayish, slimy veil that leaves a ring around the stem.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Dingy yellow to brownish cap up to 3 inches wide, distinctly slimy and slippery when wet, rounded to flattened in shape

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Small pores underneath the cap (not gills) that start bright yellow and gradually turn olive-brown as the mushroom ages

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Up to 4 inches long, decorated with distinctive reddish-brown glandular dots that feel slightly bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Ring
idTips.description: Young specimens have a grayish, slimy partial veil that ruptures and leaves a sheathlike ring around the stem

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found near pine trees, appearing scattered or in small groups on the ground, never on wood

habitat: Look for Slippery Jill on the ground near various pine species throughout New England's forests and woodlands. It forms beneficial partnerships with pine tree roots, so you'll never find it far from these conifers. It prefers well-drained forest floors and can appear in both pure pine stands and mixed forests where pines are present.

seasonality.spring: Not typically fruiting yet, though mycelium is active underground forming connections with pine roots.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season begins, especially after warm rains when the characteristic slimy caps are most noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Prime time for finding fresh specimens, particularly in late summer through early fall when conditions are consistently moist.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting ceases, but dried remnants from fall might still be visible on the forest floor.

funFact: Slippery Jill is such an effective world traveler that it has hitchhiked to six continents by forming partnerships with pine trees - when people transplant pines to new locations, the mushroom's microscopic spores often come along for the ride and establish in completely new countries!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other slippery Suillus species like Sour Cap Suillus, but Slippery Jill's reddish-brown dotted stem is a dead giveaway - think "Jill has polka-dotted stockings" to remember this key feature.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name has been a bit of a moving target - this mushroom was shuffled between different names for over a century before settling on Suillus salmonicolor in 1983, and some experts still debate whether it's truly distinct from a closely related species.
compareHints: Among its Suillus relatives, Slippery Jill stands out with its distinctive reddish-brown dotted stem - most other slippery jacks either lack these glandular dots or have different colored ones. The Dotted-stalked Suillus has similar dots but they're typically paler, while Purple-veiled Slippery Jack has a purple-tinged veil rather than grayish.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Suillus relatives, the Painted Suillus stands out dramatically with its red and yellow crackled cap pattern – most other slippery jacks have solid-colored, slimy caps in browns or yellows.

Among New England's Slippery Jacks, the Chicken Fat Mushroom stands out with its reddish-brown cap scales and consistently slimy texture - features that separate it from the Purple-veiled Slippery Jack's partial veil or the Dotted-stalked Suillus's white cap.
Unlike the Painted Suillus with its reddish streaks, or the Chicken Fat Mushroom with its more orange tones, the Butterball maintains consistent golden-butter coloring.
Unlike its cousin the Purple-veiled Slippery Jack which has a distinctive ring around the stem, the Dotted-stalked Suillus has a completely ringless stem covered in granular dots.
